about: What stood in Koʻolaupoko, from Waimānalo to Kualoa: the walled fishponds of Kāneʻohe Bay and the inland ponds of Kailua, the loʻi on the valley floors where the kuleana of the 1850s lie, the villages, heiau, paths and streams. DATA.md “District packs” gives the schema; RESEARCH.md §13 says how each feature was made. A feature’s to year is the last year a source read shows it, not a sourced end; from 2010 a restored loʻi is a feature of its own. Ponds traced from today’s heights or from the 1943 map are mapped; ponds from the State site record carry its site number; heiau carry placePrecision and ahupuaa and stand at the ahupuaʻa centroid, Ulupō, a State historic site, excepted; streams carry role reference, the mapped courses kept for labels and checks while the app routes the water from the heights.

properties.name: Moliʻi
properties.note: The pond below Kualoa, its wall running along the shore of the bay. The outline is the water inside the wall and the wall itself, traced on today’s topobathymetric heights; the 1927 sheet draws and names Moliʻi Pond in the same place, and the wall stands today. When it was built is in no source read. GNIS spells it Mōliʻi, the State site record Moliʻi; a speaker should settle it.

properties.name: Kahouna
properties.note: The walled pond on the shore of Kahaluʻu, which the State site record names Kahouna and GNIS Kahaluʻu Pond. The outline is the water inside the wall and the wall, traced on today’s heights; the 1927 sheet draws the pond beside Libbyville, and the wall stands today.

properties.name: Heʻeia
properties.note: The great walled pond of Heʻeia, its wall curving out over the reef flat from the shore. The outline is the water inside the wall and the wall, traced on today’s heights, the openings for the sluice gates closed; the 1881 sheet writes Loko here, Jackson’s chart of the bay in 1882 draws the pond, and the 1927 sheet names it Heʻeia Pond. The wall is cared for and rebuilt today.

properties.name: Oʻohope
properties.note: A small pond on the Heʻeia shore west of the hill the 1927 sheet calls Puu Pahu, outlined in the State historic site record. The 1927 sheet names Oohope Pond and the 1943 map still fills it as water; GNIS lists it as historical, so the end year is the 1943 map’s. Spelling as GNIS gives it, for a speaker to check.

properties.name: Kalokohanahou
properties.note: A pond on the Kāneʻohe shore of the bay, outlined in the State historic site record as the Kīpuka layer publishes it. Lyons’s survey of Kāneʻohe (1874) names it, the 1927 sheet draws it, and the 1943 map still fills it as water; GNIS lists it as historical, so the end year is the 1943 map’s. When it was built is in no source read.

tellings.says: Lyons’s survey of 1874 writes “7 acres fish pond Kalokohanahau” beside the land of Kalokohanahou.

properties.name: Kanohuluiwi and Waikapoki
properties.note: Two small ponds side by side on the Kāneʻohe shore between Kalokohanahou and Punaluʻu, traced as one from the blue fill of the 1943 map. Lyons’s survey of 1874 writes Kanohuluiwi here; GNIS gives Kanohuluiwi Fish Pond and Waikapoki Fish Pond (historical) at the two of them, and the State site record has an outline for Kanohuluiwi.

properties.name: Punaluʻu
properties.note: A pond on the Kāneʻohe shore of the bay, outlined in the State historic site record as the Kīpuka layer publishes it. Lyons’s survey of Kāneʻohe (1874) names it, the 1927 sheet draws it, and the 1943 map still fills it as water; GNIS lists it as historical, so the end year is the 1943 map’s. When it was built is in no source read.

tellings.says: Lyons’s survey of 1874: “fish pond to Punaluu 13¼ Acres”.
Monsarrat’s map of the Waikalua swamp, March 1896, draws Punaluu Fish Pond at its north edge.

properties.name: Waikalua Loko
properties.note: The pond at the mouth of Kāneʻohe Stream, traced from the blue fill of the 1943 map. Lyons’s survey (1874) writes “fish pond to Waikalua Loko”, Monsarrat’s map of 1896 draws Waikalua Fish Pond beside the rice of the swamp, and the 2000 sheet still draws a fishpond here; the walled basin on today’s heights is smaller than the 1943 water.

properties.name: Keana
properties.note: A small pond just east of Waikalua Loko, outlined in the State site record, which names it with its neighbours; the Kīpuka place names put Keana here. Lyons’s survey (1874) writes Loko Keana beside it and the 1943 map fills it as water.

properties.name: Mikiola, Kapuʻu and Mahinui
properties.note: Three ponds in a row on the shore below Mahinui, outlined together in the State site record (which adds the name Kaluoa). The 1927 and 1943 maps name Mikiola, Kapuu and Mahinui Pond; Lyons’s survey (1874) names the Mikiola pond and the fish pond to Mahinui. The end year is the 1943 map’s, the last read that shows them.

tellings.says: Lyons’s survey of 1874: “fish pond to Mahinui 11 Acres”, and a pond of “3 Acres” beside it.

properties.name: Keaʻalau
properties.note: A pond at Keaʻalau, at the foot of the Mōkapu side of the bay, outlined in the State site record; the 1943 map fills it as water. Lyons’s survey (1874) writes Keaalau, part of Waikalua, here.

properties.name: Nuʻupia, Halekou and Kaluapuhi
properties.note: The ponds across the neck of Mōkapu, outlined together in the State site record. Jackson’s chart of 1882 names Halekou, Nuupia and Kaluapuhi fish ponds with salt works beside them; the 1927 sheet draws the three ponds in marsh, and the 2000 sheet still draws Halekou and Nuʻupia ponds inside the air station.

tellings.says: The Mōkapu history of 1965 says the Nuʻupia area held three ponds, Halekou and Nuʻupia west of the road and Kaluapuhi east of it, and that it was “nearly 300 acres in size” at the turn of the century (pp. 15–16).

properties.name: Kawainui
properties.note: The great inland pond of Kailua, behind the beach, divided from Kaʻelepulu by a low stone wall. The outline is the State site record’s, which is the marsh the pond became; the 1927 sheet writes Kawainui Swamp across the same ground. Kamakau has Kamehameha working at its ponds in his years on Oʻahu, and by the late 1820s bulrushes had overgrown most of it, so the end year is the late 1820s of that account.

tellings.says: State Parks describes Kawainui about 1750 as a fishpond of about 400 acres, with mullet, awa and ʻoʻopu.
The freshwater pond may have been in use as early as the late seventeenth century; by the late 1820s the main part of the wetland was dominated by bulrushes (p. 35).

properties.name: Kaʻelepulu
properties.note: The second inland pond of Kailua, between Kawainui and the sea, outlined in the State site record with the marsh around it. The 1881 sheet writes Kaeleoulu Loko, the 1927 sheet Kaelepulu Pond, and the 1943 map still fills the pond in its marsh. From the mid-1960s the houses of Enchanted Lake were built around it, so the end year is the 1943 map’s.

properties.name: Pāhonu
properties.note: The walled pond on the Waimānalo shore where, in tradition, turtles were kept for the chiefs. The State site record places it at the shore by Kaiona; its wall shows on neither today’s heights nor the old sheets, so the outline is a drawn half-ring on the reef flat at that point, its size a guess. Its wall is being rebuilt today.

properties.name: Loʻi of Hakipuʻu
properties.note: The valley floor where the kuleana awarded by the Land Commission in the early 1850s lie, as the Kīpuka award layer maps them: the small awards gathered, kept where today’s ground is gentle and low, and joined where they adjoin. The awards hold house lots and dry plots as well as loʻi, and the layer records no use, so the outline is the floor the awards cover rather than the patches themselves. The awards of the 1850s are the last record read of these patches; the end year is theirs.

properties.name: Loʻi of Heʻeia
properties.note: The valley floor where the kuleana awarded by the Land Commission in the early 1850s lie, as the Kīpuka award layer maps them: the small awards gathered, kept where today’s ground is gentle and low, and joined where they adjoin. properties.name: Loʻi of Heʻeia, restored
properties.note: The loʻi kalo brought back on the Heʻeia wetland from 2010 by Kākoʻo ʻŌiwi, on its lease of the State’s wetland parcel, whose farm lies beside the highway just south of the Heʻeia Stream bridge. The patch is drawn there at about the area its history gives, not surveyed.

tellings.says: Since 2010 Kākoʻo ʻŌiwi has restored about six acres of loʻi kalo and cleared about twenty acres more for dryland crops.

properties.name: Kailua
properties.note: The houses of the chiefs, their families and attendants around Kailua Bay, as State Parks describes the place about 1750. The point is the GNIS point for Kailua; no source read bounds the village. By 1850 the land’s people lived in several clusters, Maunawili among them.

tellings.says: Kailua ahupuaʻa held about 610 people in 1850, down from 762 in the missionary census of 1835–36; nearly 180 lived in the Maunawili region, one of four clusters (p. 35). No count of households.
No count. Kākuhihewa’s great house Pamoa stood at Alele in Kailua (p. 274).

properties.name: Kāneʻohe
properties.note: The village by the shore of the bay where the mission station stood from the 1830s. The point is where the 1881 sheet writes “Old Mission Res. & Church”; Lyons’s survey of 1874 has the mission’s land, the church, a court house and many small kuleana here, the last source read to show the village as such.

tellings.says: No count. At Kāneʻohe the people built a small thatched church for the new station in 1834 (p. 467).
No count of households. The Kīpuka award layer maps about 250 parcels awarded in Kāneʻohe, most in the early 1850s, under about 136 claims.

properties.name: Kukui
properties.note: A small fishing village on the Waimānalo shore near Pāhonu. In 1794 the Oʻahu chiefs dug trenches and threw up earthworks at Kukui against Kaʻeokūlani. The point is a marker near Pāhonu; no source read bounds the village.

tellings.says: No count. “The small fishing village of Kukui” lay along the bay “in the Kaiona Beach vicinity near Pahonu Pond” (p. 27).

properties.name: Ulupō
properties.note: The great terraced platform at the edge of Kawainui, a State historic site open to the public. Tradition credits its stonework to the menehune; it may have begun as a heiau for the crops of Kawainui. Thrum’s list has an Upo at Kailua, stone-paved and still standing, probably the same.

tellings.says: Ulupō measures 140 by 180 feet, with walls up to 30 feet high, and was probably abandoned by 1795.

properties.name: Pahukini
properties.note: A heiau on the west side of Kawainui, on the slopes above the marsh.

properties.name: Holomakani
properties.note: A heiau on the west side of Kawainui. Kamakau tells of travellers from Kahiki who landed at Mōkapu, whose names, Olomana, Aniani and Holomakani, are still found in Koʻolaupoko.

properties.name: Alala
properties.note: The heiau at Kailua where the rites for the birth of Kūaliʻi were held and the sacred drums Opuku and Hawea were brought, as Fornander prints them. Spelling as Fornander and Thrum print it, for a speaker to check.

properties.name: Kawaewae
properties.note: A heiau of Kāneʻohe, of doubtful size and class in Thrum’s list, which credits it to Olopana; Lyons’s survey (1874) writes Kawaewae as a land of Kāneʻohe.

properties.name: Olohana
properties.note: A heiau of Waimānalo in Thrum’s list, of which he obtained no particulars.

properties.name: Pueo
properties.note: A heiau of Waimānalo in Thrum’s list, of which he obtained no particulars.

properties.name: The way down to Kāneʻohe Bay
properties.note: From the foot of the pali north across Kāneʻohe to the shore of the bay at Mahinui, along the road of the 1881 sheet. Bingham went down the pali into Koʻolau in the early 1820s and Ellis came up it; no source read says where the older path ran below the pali.

properties.name: The way to Maunawili
properties.note: From below the pali east to Maunawili, along the road of the 1881 sheet toward Waimānalo; no source read says the older path ran exactly here.
